en: Now begins the seventy-first chapter: On the Life-Span Calculation by the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭavarga*).
Now, I shall here declare the lifespan arising from the eight divisions (aṣṭavarga):
two days for a line with no marks (virekhā), and one and a half days for a single line.
In a [line] with two lines, it lasts for one day; in a line with three lines, for half a day;
and in lines equal to the Vedas (four), it is recorded as lasting seven and a half days.
With five lines, it indicates two years; with six lines, four equal years;
with seven lines, six years; and with eight lines, eight years. (3)
Thus, when the lifespan derived from all the planets has been obtained,
half of that shall be the clear lifespan of men arising from the aṣṭavarga.
Now begins the seventy-second chapter: On the Aṣṭakavarga of the Collective [Planets].
One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel joined with the signs beginning from the natal ascendant;
having combined all the results of the *aṣṭakas*, one should assign them to each spoke. || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born, this group of eight is declared to denote a collective whole; therefore, the results for those born [under these signs] are to be understood accordingly.
Those zodiac signs whose results exceed thirty are bestowers of auspiciousness;
those with results from twenty-five up to thirty are considered to yield middling results. (3)
Therefore, those zodiac signs whose fruits have been exhausted bestow painful suffering; a wise man should join them with signs that yield excellent auspicious results.
O best of the twice-born, one should avoid malefic signs for auspicious undertakings;
a planet situated in an excellent sign is auspicious, whereas in any other, it bestows inauspicious results. (5)

Having observed the results of the houses from the body (the first house) up to the end of the twelfth, one should know that when [the strength] is greater, it is auspicious; when it is less, one should predict loss.
One should declare the middling result arising from each respective house when [the strength] is middling;
when it exceeds the middling, there is gain, and after gain, expenditure follows when it has diminished.
He for whom the ascendant (lagna) possesses an abundance of results is indeed possessed of enjoyments and wealth;
by the opposite, poverty certainly arises—of this there is no doubt.
Having divided the ten houses here into three sections, the wise man should observe which one is occupied by malefic planets; he should declare that section to be fraught with suffering.

One should declare the results to be auspicious when joined with benefics, and mixed results when joined with mixed planets; one should state the results of the three segments according to the stages of life, beginning with childhood.
If a month is marked by seven lines, there is danger of death for men;
one should give twenty palas of gold and two handfuls of sesame seeds.
When a month is marked by eight lines, a man falls under the power of death;
to prevent the destruction of his results, he should offer a balance made of camphor.
One should predict fear of serpents during the month joined with nine lines;
for the attainment of auspiciousness, one should give a chariot yoked with four horses.
In a month marked by ten lines, there is likewise fear of weapons;
therefore, one should offer the armor joined with the vajra to obtain auspicious results.
O twice-born one, where there is fear of a curse, one should offer an image of the Moon fashioned from gold, with lines [drawn] like those of Rudra and the guardians of the directions. || 15 ||
If [the water] is joined with twelve lines, one should declare fear of death;
however, by giving land abounding in crops to a Brahmin, auspicious results will arise. || 16 ||
Likewise, from lines that measure out the universe, there arises fear of death from tigers;
therefore, one should perform the gift of Viṣṇu and Hiraṇyagarbha for the attainment of auspiciousness.
In a month marked by lines measured by a hundred [units], there is fear of death;
one should give a statue of Varāha fashioned from gold.
O twice-born one, if there is fear of the king on that lunar day, one should give an elephant;
likewise, if there is misfortune for sixteen years, one should give an image of the Kalpataru tree.
Seven Indus (months) bring fear of disease; one should give a cow and molasses as a gift.
Eight Indus bring quarrels; one should give gems, cattle, land, and gold.
With twenty-one [verses], there shall be sojourn abroad; one should perform propitiation according to the prescribed rite.
With twenty [verses], there shall be loss of intellect; in that case, one should worship Gaṇeśa. (21)
If afflicted by the twenty-one types of diseases, one should give a mountain of grain;
if afflicted by Yama or the Aśvins, there is suffering for kinsmen, O twice-born, and one should give a mirror.
In the month conjoined with the twenty-third [tithi], one may encounter affliction;
therefore, a wise man should offer a golden image of the Sun weighing seven palas.
A king who is friendless and deprived of his horses and elephants should give ten buffaloes;
for the sake of destroying all diseases, he should perform recitation, fire-oblations, and other such rites. (24)
If there are twenty-five [lines], there is loss of intellect; then Vāgīśvarī is to be worshipped.
If there are twenty-six, there will be loss of wealth; the wise man should give gold.
And likewise, one should recite the Śrīsūkta twenty-seven times therein;
if it is joined with twenty-eight, there will be a loss of all kinds month after month.
The Sūryahoma should be performed according to the prescribed rite by those desiring auspiciousness;
even with twenty-nine [offerings], one may become agitated in mind. || 27 ||
A wise person should give ghee, clothing, and gold there;
by thirty [of these], one obtains a full measure of grain—such is the determination of the Jātaka. (28)
With lines exceeding thirty, there is the attainment of wealth, sons, and happiness;
and with those exceeding forty, merit and glory increase. (29)
Those who are purified by the Aṣṭavarga are pure for all rites;
therefore, purification by means of the Aṣṭavarga is desired in all rites. (30)
The *gocara* should be sought only so long as the *aṣṭavarga* has not been obtained;
once the *aṣṭavarga* is fully attained, the *gocara* becomes fruitless. || 31 ||
Now begins the chapter on the results of rays (Raśmiphala). 73.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall declare the rays of the planets: for the Sun, they are nine, five, five, seven, eight, and five; and at its exaltation, it has twelve rays. (1)
The rays (kalās) within the interval between the apogee and the planet are stated by proportion;
however, if the planet minus the apogee exceeds half a circle, one should subtract it from the full circle. || 2 ||
One should divide the [longitude] struck by its own rays by six; thus shall one's own rays be obtained. Regarding this, another specific refinement has been stated as follows: || 3 ||
In its own exaltation sign, they are tripled; in its own trine, they are doubled;
in its own house, they are multiplied by three and divided by two; and likewise in the house of a great friend. (4)
The six factors, beginning with peace (mitra), are divided by four and then multiplied by five;
likewise, if the revenues are diminished in the enemy's territory, they are divided by five. (5)

If the other lunar mansions (tārāgrahas), excluding Saturn and Venus, have set in the house of the enemy, they are doubled and divided by five; if they have set in a neutral house, they remain as they are. || 6 ||
O twice-born one, they should be understood as having powerful rays that produce clear results;
thus, the wise should declare the outcome based on the conjunction of the rays. || 7 ||
If the number of rays is from one up to five, then even those born into an excellent family become poor and tormented by suffering. (8)
From the tenth [year] onwards, men on earth are born poor, burdened by debt, and deprived of wife, children, and home.
In the eleventh [period], men will have few sons and little wealth;
in the twelfth, they will have little wealth, and will be rogues, fools, and weak.
If there are thirteen rays, they are constantly devoted to acts of theft;
if fourteen, they are righteous souls and supporters of their families. (11)
Devoted to the duties appropriate to his lineage, endowed with wealth and learning,
he was possessed of all the qualities of knowledge through his fifteen rays.
The Lord Vidhi has declared that one who is the chief of his own lineage and possesses wealth is a true householder;
moreover, those who are lords of their families have many servants. (13)
All people will be full of fame and gradually become happy;
if there are fifty rulers of the land, there will be twenty-one rays.
If he is endowed with generosity and morality, possessed of compassion, and endowed with happiness, there are twenty-two rays;
if he is gentle in character, there are twenty-three rays. (15)
Beyond thirty [years], he becomes illustrious, endowed with all virtues, beloved by kings, radiant, and surrounded by many people. (16)
Beyond this, however, a *sāmanta* (feudatory) is one who supports from one hundred people up to forty thousand, with a maximum limit of forty *karas*. || 17 ||
Beyond this, O protector of the earth, up to fifty elephants;
and beyond that, O Brahmin, a king becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) by virtue of his elephants.
Thus, one should declare the results for a newborn according to the Kula lineage, based on the planetary positions arising at the time of birth. (19)
A Kṣatriya is born as a universal monarch (cakravartin), a Vaiśya as a king,
and a Śūdra as a wealthy Brāhmaṇa devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites.
The rays of a planet facing its exaltation bestow full results;
those of a planet facing its fall bestow results less than that. || 21 ||
O twice-born one, for all planets in this manner, according to the power of their rays,
there arises for embodied beings a result that is either auspicious or inauspicious.
Without knowledge of the rays, one cannot correctly understand the result;
therefore, the wise must first establish the rays before declaring the result. (23)
Now begins the chapter on the results of the Sudarśana-cakra, [Chapter] 74.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall declare this supreme secret knowledge for the benefit of the worlds, which was spoken by Brahmā himself. (1)
By means of the discus named Sudarśana, the astrologer is able to clearly know the results of the houses, beginning with the body, for human beings. (2)
Listen with a single-minded focus to all that arises from birth until death—occurring over years, months, and days—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. (3)
O twice-born one, one should draw three beautiful circles originating from a single center;
one should then fashion twelve spokes therein, and thus the Sudarśana [mandala] is formed.
There, in the first circle, the houses beginning with the ascendant should be written along with their planets;
above that, in the second circle, the houses starting from the Moon should be written together with the planets. || 5 ||
From the Sun, the planets situated in their respective orbits above it appear in succession; thus, in each individual sign here, there shall be three signs for the solar mansions.

But here, the first house is determined by the sum of the ascendant, the moon, and the sun; having established that as the body (the first house), the subsequent houses, beginning with wealth, are to be understood.
In each respective case, the wise should understand the corresponding result based on the position of the planet.
When the Sun is in the first house (the ascendant), it is to be known as auspicious; elsewhere, it bestows inauspicious results.
Even a malefic planet situated in its own exaltation sign does not bestow inauspicious results;
thus, having observed both the auspicious and inauspicious aspects, one should declare the results for each respective house.
Whatever house is conjoined with or aspected by its own lord or a benefic planet prospers;
however, for that which is conjoined with or aspected by malefic planets, loss occurs. (10)
The result for a house occupied by a planet is equal to the result of a planetary conjunction;
however, for a house not occupied by a planet, the result is equal to the aspect of a planet. || 11 ||
From auspicious planets alone, an auspicious result arises; from malefic planets, an inauspicious one; and from mixed planets, a mixed result.
When the auspicious are predominant, it should be known as auspicious; when the inauspicious are predominant, it is inauspicious.
O best of the twice-born, having thus observed the conjunctions and aspects of the planets upon the houses, the results should be declared according to their relative degrees of strength.
Where there is no planet at all and no aspect for anyone, then that result arising from its state should be known according to the influence of its own lord. 14.
Even an auspicious [planet], when among a preponderance of inauspicious divisions, bestows inauspicious results;
even an inauspicious [planet], when among a preponderance of auspicious divisions, bestows auspicious results. (15)

In this system, the six divisions (ṣaḍvarga) of one's own [sign], of an exalted sign, and of a benefic sign are to be known as bringing auspicious results; whereas the six divisions of an enemy sign, a malefic sign, and a debilitated sign bestow inauspicious results. (16)
O best of the twice-born, in this same manner, one should consider the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of all the planets and their various states, and then predict the resulting effects.
When the fruit of the body is accomplished from the *sudarśana* [ascendant] alone, then why is it that all the sages have declared the fruit to arise from the *lagna* [ascendant] itself? (18)
Thus, this doubt has arisen in me; it ought to be resolved:
when the Sun and the Moon are situated separately from the ascendant, each in a different sign. (19)
Then, the results from the Sudarśana-cakra should be declared by the wise;
if there are one, two, or three [planets] in a single sign, then one should declare the results from the ascendant.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall declare the results arising from each year and so forth,
derived from this very Sudarśana [cakra] according to the influence of the periods (daśās) and sub-periods (antaradaśās).
One should calculate the years as one, two and a half, and three [from] the body (tanu) and so forth;
one should allot the periods (daśās) of the twelve houses beginning with the lord of the year within those years. || 22 ||
Likewise, the sub-periods (antardaśās) and so forth [of those planets] are determined; their results in months and other periods are according to their strengths.
O twice-born one, having assigned the respective houses as numerical values, [the results] arise from each of those signs and so forth. (23)
Benefic planets situated in a quadrant, a trine, or the eighth house from that particular ascendant bestow auspicious results;
however, wherever Rāhu may be located, it causes the destruction of that house.
Wherever there are many malefic planets, there occurs the destruction of that particular state;
however, it is auspicious when malefics are situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses along with strong benefics.
In this manner, one should contemplate the results of the various houses for every year and month;
and within the lifespan, one should calculate the periods (daśās) by repeating the twelve-fold cycle.
Thus, having understood the results arising from the year, month, and so forth from the Sudarśana-cakra,
as well as those arising from the Aṣṭavarga, the determination of the result is made by means of both.
For when there is equality in both, one should declare that fruit to be complete;
when there is inequality, that fruit which is predominant [arises] according to the sequence of their strengths.
Now begins the chapter on the characteristics of the five great men (Pañcamahāpuruṣalakṣaṇādhyāya), [chapter] 75.

Now I shall describe the characteristics of the five great men (mahāpuruṣa), which arise when Mars and the other planets are strong and situated in their own signs, exaltations, or angular houses (kendras). || 1 ||
Kramaśa, Rucaka, Bhadra, Haṃsa, and Mālavya, as well as Śaśa—all these are considered great men by all the wise. (2)
Long-faced, greatly energetic, possessing the luster of the sun, and exceedingly powerful; with beautiful eyebrows and dark hair, he was highly resplendent and fond of battle. || 3 ||
He is reddish-dark in complexion, the slayer of enemies, the knower of mantras, and the leader of thieves;
he is cruel, the protector of men, with slender feet, and a worshiper of the twice-born.
His hands are marked with the lute, the vajra, the bow, the noose, the bull, and the wheel;
he is skilled in mantras and sorcery, and his height is exactly one hundred finger-breadths.
O best of the twice-born, its middle part is declared by the wise to be equal in length to its mouth; such a *rucaka* is equal to a thousand *tulās*.
He enjoys the region of the Vindhya and Sahya mountains for seventy years;
then, whether by the sword or by fire, he goes to the abode of the gods.
A man with the prowess of a tiger, broad-chested, with the gait of an elephant,
with thick calves and arms, wise, and well-proportioned, is a knower of Yoga.
He is of the nature of sattva, possessed of beautiful feet and endowed with handsome facial hair;
he is full of desire and marked by the symbols of the conch, mace, discus, arrow, and elephant.
His lotus-like hands and feet were marked with the signs of the banner and the plow;
he possessed a beautiful nose, was learned in the scriptures, steadfast, and bore dark, curly hair.
He is independent in all his undertakings and capable of pleasing his own kin; he enjoys sovereignty constantly, both with his own friends and with those of others. (11)
Weighed on a scale and measured by its weight, along with his wife and son, the king shall rule the Middle Country in safety for a hundred years. (12)
He is swan-like, with the voice of a swan, fair-complexioned, with a beautiful face and a prominent nose;
he is phlegmatic, with honey-colored tawny eyes, red-colored nails, and is highly intelligent.
The king has full cheeks, rounded veins, and beautiful feet;
he is marked with the signs of a fish, a goad, a bow, a conch, a lotus, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
One whose hands and feet bear auspicious marks, who is afflicted by passion for women, does not attain contentment;
however, one sixty-nine finger-breadths in height, who delights in water-sports, is happy.
He protects the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā for a hundred years,
and having enjoyed every happiness on earth, he meets his end at the edge of a forest.
A man with even lips, a slender waist, and the luster of the moon;
fragrant, with limbs that are neither too red, nor too short, nor too tall—(is auspicious). || 17 ||
He has the gait of an elephant in rut, arms reaching down to his knees,
and a face measuring twelve fingers in length and ten fingers in width.
Mālavya protects the region known as Mālava together with the Sindhu;
having enjoyed happiness until the end of seventy years, he goes to the excellent abode.
With slender teeth and face, brave, neither too short nor thin-waisted, lean in the middle, with beautiful shanks, he is intelligent and a knower of the vulnerabilities of others. (20)
He is capable in forests and mountain strongholds; he is a leader of armies, formidable, and like a hare [in agility]; he is fickle, an alchemist, devoted to women, and endowed with other powers.
With his hands and feet marked by lines of garlands, lutes, drums, and weapons,
this king protects the earth while living happily for as long as the mountains endure.
Now begins the chapter on the results of the five great elements (Pañcamahābhūta-phalādhyāya), [Chapter] 76.
Now I shall explain to you the knowledge of the shadow of the five great elements (pañcamahābhūtacchāyājñāna), by which the current planetary periods (daśā) of the planets are known by the wise. (1)
Mars and the other planets are the lords of fire, earth, water, and air respectively;
it should be understood that the results arising from those elements depend on the strength of their respective [rulers]. (2)
If Mars is weak, a man is born with the nature of fire;
if Mercury, he will have the nature of earth; and if Jupiter, the nature of space.
In Venus, there is the nature of water; in Saturn, the nature of wind;
and through a mixture [of these], O best of the twice-born, a mixed nature is to be understood.
The Sun possesses the nature of fire, and the Moon has the essence of water;
during their respective periods, these planets manifest the qualities born of their own elements.
Afflicted by hunger, fickle, brave, emaciated, wise, and gluttonous; sharp, fair-bodied, proud, and of a fiery temperament is such a man. (6)
A man born under the Mahī-nakṣatra is rich in camphor, lotuses, and perfumes; he is a seeker of enjoyments, possesses stable happiness, is strong, patient, and has a lion-like roar.
He is a knower of words and their meanings, skilled in ethics, bold, and endowed with wisdom;
he has a wide-open mouth and is exceedingly tall, being born from the nature of space.
One born from the nature of water is radiant, capable of bearing burdens, pleasant of speech, a lord of the earth, possessing many friends, gentle, and wise.
A person born with a predominance of the air element (vāyu-tattva) becomes a donor, irascible, fair-complexioned, fond of wandering, a king, difficult to overcome, and thin-limbed. || 10 ||
A golden luster, auspicious vision, the accomplishment of all undertakings and purposes, victory, and the acquisition of wealth arise when the Moon is in the sign of Leo (Vahni). || 11 ||
When there is a pleasant fragrance on the body, the nails and teeth are very glossy, and there is the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, this is the shadow of the earth. (12)
The shadow arising from one's own face or from the sky bestows eloquence of speech;
there, happiness born from hearing beautiful sounds arises. (13)
When there is softness and well-being in the body, like the reflection of the moon in water, then the embodied being experiences the pleasure of tasting the desired flavor. (14)
Dirtiness, delusion, demonic possession, and disease arise from the wind;
likewise, grief and torment occur when the wind is in excess. (15)
Thus, O twice-born one, the wise should understand the results when Mars and the other planets are strong; when they are weak, the results should be declared in the opposite manner.
One should declare the opposite result when [the planets] occupy low or inimical houses;
the attainment of results through weak planets occurs in dreams. (17)
Furthermore, for the sake of pacifying the evil results of those whose births are unknown,
the current period (daśā) of the planets is to be understood by the ripening of their fruits.
Now begins the chapter on the results of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest. || 77 ||
Moreover, O twice-born one, I shall describe the results according to the influence of the qualities (guṇas):
one born when a Sattvic planet is rising will be exceedingly virtuous and highly intelligent. || 1 ||
When a planet of the nature of *rajas* rises, the wise man born will be endowed with the quality of *rajas*;
when a planet of the nature of *tamas* rises, the one born will be a fool, dominated by *tamas*.
One born when the planets are in a state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) is endowed with that same equilibrium;
thus, O Brahmin, four types of beings are born upon this earth.
I shall describe their qualities—superior, middling, inferior, and indifferent—in due order, as they were spoken by Nārada and others. || 4 ||
Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and straightforwardness;
lack of greed, and truthfulness—these are the virtues found in a person of superior character. (5)
Valor, splendor, fortitude, dexterity, not fleeing in battle,
and the protection of the virtuous— these qualities are to be known as predominant in those characterized by rajas.
Greed, untruthfulness, dullness, laziness,
and skill in the service of others— these are the qualities when tamas predominates.
Skill in agriculture, commerce, and cattle-rearing;
the ability to speak both truth and falsehood—these are the qualities found in one of balanced temperament.
O best of Brahmins, one should employ that person— whether superior, middling, inferior, or indifferent— in accordance with the characteristics by which they are defined within that particular task.
O best of the twice-born, when one [quality] exceeds the other two, that excess is declared; otherwise, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) is to be understood.
Thus, between the served and the server, as well as between the maiden and the groom, affection remains steadfast only when they are equal in their qualities. (11)

O Brahmin, for one who is indifferent, the inferior person acts as a refuge for joy; likewise, for the indifferent one, the middling person acts as such; and for the middling one, the superior person becomes a refuge for delight. 12.
Therefore, a maiden inferior to one's wife is inferior, and a servant inferior to one's wife is inferior;
from such [inferiority] in qualities arises unhappiness, whereas otherwise there is indeed loss.
Vigor is the field for procreation, and likewise, the proper time and the union are the causes;
each subsequent factor is more powerful than the preceding one as a cause for qualities such as excellence.
Therefore, the quality in a birth chart (jātaka) is similar to the time of birth;
having examined that, the wise should declare the results. 15.
Time creates beings, maintains them, and also withdraws them;
it is the Lord, the imperishable, blessed, and all-pervading master of all worlds.
That power is declared by the sages to be Prakṛti, consisting of the three guṇas;
though unmanifest, it becomes manifest to embodied beings when thus divided.
Its four constituent parts arise from its own qualities in four ways: the highest, the middling, the indifferent, and the lowest, respectively. (18)
In an excellent [family], a superior person is born; in a middling one, a middling person;
in a neutral one, a neutral person; and in an inferior one, an inferior person is born. (19)
The head is the highest part of his body, the chest is the middle part,
the two shanks are the indifferent part, and the feet are said to be the lowest.
Thus, by the power of qualities alone, the distinction of time arises;
and from that distinction, the distinction of species arises here among the moving and the unmoving.
Thus was this fourfold world created by the Lord, the All-pervading One, together with his own qualities and the fourfold time.
Now begins the chapter on the lost horoscope (Naṣṭajātakādhyāya). || 78 ||
O Sage, you have thus described the results that arise solely from the power of the time of birth;
however, how is the result to be known for one whose time of birth is unknown? (1)
Whether it be auspicious or even inauspicious, whatever was previously done by a human being—if there exists any remedy for it, you ought to speak of that. (2)
Well asked by you, O Brahmin, whose mind is intent on the welfare of the world!
Out of affection for you, I shall describe the fruit of those whose births are unknown.
Whatever remains unknown regarding the years, solstices, seasons, months, fortnights, lunar days, asterisms, and so forth, that measurement is known through the ascendant of the query.
If Jupiter is situated in the sign that corresponds to the twelfth-part of the question, one should declare a birth;
the solstice is northern if it is in the first half of the ascendant, and southern if it is in the latter half. (5)
The seasons, beginning with the summer, are determined by the lords of the season, the ascendant, the decan, and the lunar mansion;
summer is assigned to Saturn, Venus, Mars, the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Sun respectively. (6)
But in the case of a conflict between the solstices and the seasons, Mercury, the Moon, and Jupiter must be mutually exchanged with Mars, Venus, and Saturn.

O twice-born one, the month is known from the first half of the *dṛkāṇa*, while the other [half] belongs to the latter [half]; the lunar day (*tithi*) should be determined by proportion, equal to the degrees of the sun.
By virtue of that, whatever desired time is equal to the time of birth, one should determine the planets and the houses therein and declare its results. || 9 ||
When the Guru returns to that same zodiac sign after twelve years,
O Sage, in which year of his cycle should that be known to occur?
O best of the twice-born, when there is doubt regarding the year, one should add twelve and twelve [years] there based on the inference from the age of the questioner.
If doubt still arises even there, the preceptor should be considered as being in the ascendant or its trine;
then, the year should be determined as before by means of an inference based on age.
"O Blessed One, having understood that a month consists of [thirty] solar parts, how does the knowledge of time come to be? Please tell me this with a mind intent on favoring the world. (13)

O best of the twice-born, on the day equal to the desired solar parts at the next transit, the sunrise value of the sun is to be calculated; the difference between that and the desired sun [is the required correction]. (14)
Having converted [the degrees] into *kalās* and multiplied by six, divide by the true motion of the sun;
the result, in measures of *ghaṭīs* and so forth, is the duration from sunrise onwards. (15)

The time of the desired [solar] revolution in the previous birth should indeed be known by the wise in due order; having calculated the [longitude of the] sun at sunrise, one should subtract the elapsed revolutions from the desired sun. (16)
Now begins the chapter on the application of the religious life (pravrajyāyoga), [chapter] 79.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall explain the yoga known as renunciation (pravrajya),
by which people depart from their home toward another stage of life.
With four or more planets situated together and possessing strength, one attains ordination;
with the Sun and others [in such positions], one becomes an ascetic, a skull-bearer, or a wearer of red garments.
The Ekadaṇḍī ascetic, the Cakradhara, and the Nirgranthika are to be known, in that order, as belonging only to one who possesses superior vigor, even among many who possess strength. (3)
Even if they are endowed with valor, if they have set with the sun, those people should be known as uninitiated, despite their devotion to him. (4)
O best of the twice-born, when the planets have set and are weak while the Sun is strong, then the Pravrajyā yoga arising from the Sun should be known.
If the lord of the birth sign is not aspected by other planets but is aspected by Saturn,
then by the strength of those two, a man shall attain renunciation there.
If the lord of the birth sign is weak and aspected by Saturn alone,
then that person will attain renunciation specifically through the state of Saturn.
When the Moon is situated in a Navāṃśa of Saturn or Mars within a Dreṣkāṇa of Saturn,
and is aspected by Saturn, renunciation (pravrajyā) arising from Saturn should be known to occur.
Venus is victorious over Mars and the other planets whether situated in the north or even in the south;
likewise, another planet situated in the north is victorious, and they become mutually joined when they meet one another. || 9 ||
If the one who has undertaken the life of renunciation is defeated by another, like spittle, then he abandons that renunciation which he had obtained, and takes it up again.
If many planets that cause renunciation are present at the time of birth and are equal in strength, then what kind of renunciation would there be in that case? (11)
If many powerful planets should be the causers of renunciation, then one certainly attains the state of renunciation from all of them. || 12 ||
During the period of each respective planet's influence, a person born under it enters the life of a wandering ascetic;
having abandoned the previously adopted state, that human being attains another.

When the Moon, Jupiter, and the Ascendant are aspected by Saturn, and Jupiter is in the ninth house, one born here in this royal yoga becomes a founder of a religious sect; of this there is no doubt. (14)
When Saturn has reached the ninth house (dharmasthāna) and is devoid of planetary aspects, one born here in a Rājayoga shall become an initiated king. || 15 ||
Now begins the chapter on the birth-horoscopes of women (Strījātaka). || 80 ||
O Sage, you have explained in many ways the results of birth (jātaka);
tell me now how those [results] for women are to be understood.
"O Brahmin, you have asked well; I shall therefore explain that as well.
It has been stated by the wise that the fruit for women is to be understood as being equal to that of men."
I shall briefly describe the specific distinction observed therein:
the results for the body are found in the ascendant, and likewise, birth is determined by the fifth house. (3)

O twice-born one, whatever result for women— whether it be the good fortune of a husband or widowhood— is indicated in the seventh house or the eighth house, one should declare that same result to apply to their husband.
That woman whose Ascendant and Moon are in even signs remains established in her true nature;
she is endowed with qualities befitting a maiden, possesses excellent character, and bears auspicious marks.
If she is aspected by a benefic planet, she is beautiful and always endowed with physical comfort;
if aspected by a malefic, she has a masculine form and is ill-behaved.
If both [the Ascendant and the Moon] are full of evil and devoid of virtues, one should declare mixed results when they are mixed.
Whichever of the two—the Ascendant or the Moon—is stronger, its results will manifest especially so.

O Brahmin, whichever is stronger between the Ascendant and the Moon, the results for women—especially so—should be declared based on the thirty-degree divisions (triṃśāṃśas) occupied by them or according to the zodiac signs of those planets. (8)
If Mars is in its own triṃśāṃśa, the maiden will be wicked in her father's house;
likewise, she is remembered as being of bad character when Venus is in the same position, and as being well-behaved when Mercury is there.
If [the Moon] is in a sign of Jupiter, she is virtuous; in Saturn's, a servant; in Mercury's, fickle;
in Venus's, she is promiscuous; and in a portion of Mercury's, she is endowed with virtues.
If she is in the portion of the Sun, she is impotent; in that of Jupiter, she is wicked;
in that of Venus, she is renowned for her virtues; and in that of Mercury, she will be skilled in the arts. || 11 ||

If Jupiter is in its own sign, she is virtuous; if Mars is there, she is a remarried woman; if the Moon is there, she is independent; if Mars is in its thirty-degree division (atriṃśāṃśa), she is a disgrace to her family; and if Venus is there, she is likewise a blemish to her lineage.

If [the Moon] is in Baudha (Mercury), she is skilled in the arts and crafts; in Jaiva (Jupiter), she possesses many virtues; in Śanau (Saturn), she is a destroyer of her husband; in Arkabha (the Sun), she is talkative; and in Kauje (Mars) or Bhārgave (Venus), she is a chaste wife.
If [the moon] is in Baudha (Mercury), she is active like a man; in Jaiva (Jupiter), she is a queen; in Mānda (Saturn), she has fallen from her family;
in Kauja (Mars), she possesses many virtues; in Āryarkṣa (Venus), she is considered unchaste. || 14 ||
In the house of Mercury she is endowed with discernment; in that of Jupiter, she is possessed of many virtues;
in that of Saturn, she is said to have little interest; and likewise in the sign of Mars or the Sun, she is a servant.

In the house of Venus, she is highly wise; likewise, in that of Mercury, she is ill-placed and wicked. In the house of Jupiter, she is said to be devoted to her husband; in that of Saturn, she follows base people. (16)

If Mandi is in an empty house and not aspected by benefics, the husband will be a coward; if it is in a movable sign, he will be a traveler; and if Mandi is there with Jupiter, he will be impotent. (17)
If the Sun is set, she is abandoned by her husband; if Mars is there, she becomes a widow in childhood;
and if Saturn aspects it inauspiciously, the girl reaches old age as a virgin. (18)

If malefic planets are situated in the seventh house from the ascendant, she is a widow; if they are benefic, she is a virtuous wife; if there are mixed planets, she is known as a remarried woman (punaḥbhū), endowed with mixed results. || 19 ||
If Venus and Mars are situated in each other's signs, then the woman is attached to another;
and if the Moon is situated in the seventh house, she acts with her husband's permission.
If Venus or Saturn, along with the Moon and Venus, are situated in the ascendant, then that woman will certainly become an unchaste woman together with her mother. || 21 ||
If Mars or its navāṃśa is set, the husband will be lustful toward women and prone to anger;
likewise, if Mercury or its navāṃśa is so placed, he will be learned, skilled in the arts, and wise.
If [the Moon] is in Jupiter's sign, you will have a husband endowed with all virtues and one who has conquered his senses;
if in Venus's sign, he will be possessed of good fortune, handsome, and beloved by women. (23)

If [the Moon] is in a sign of Saturn or in a Navamsha of Saturn, one is old and foolish; if it is in the seventh house, one is exceedingly mild; and if it is in a Navamsha of the Sun or in that very sign, one is a performer of great deeds.
If Cancer or its Navamsha is present, the husband will be charming, lustful, and gentle;
if there is a mixture of signs, mixed results should be predicted according to the relative strength of the signs and their Navamshas.
If the Sun has reached the eighth house at birth, the woman will be joined with suffering and poverty;
she will have wounded limbs, be full of distress, and be averse to dharma.
When the Moon has gone to the eighth house, a woman becomes ill-favored, with deformed breasts and distorted eyes;
she is destitute of clothing and ornaments, afflicted by disease, and exceedingly contemptible. (27)
If Mars is situated in the eighth house, the young woman will have a lean body, be afflicted by disease, be a widow, lack luster, and be distressed by grief and suffering. (28)
Born when [the Moon] has gone to the sign of Mercury, she is devoid of righteousness, afflicted by fear, destitute of the wealth of self-respect, lacking in virtues, and fond of quarreling. (29)
If Jupiter is in the eighth house, the young woman will be lacking in virtuous conduct, have few offspring, engage in much idle talk, be abandoned by her husband, and be a heavy eater.
If Venus has gone to the eighth house, the woman born will be negligent, devoid of wealth, merciless, lacking in righteousness, filthy, and full of deceit. || 31 ||
A woman born when Saturn occupies the eighth house will be of wicked nature, a thief, intent on deception, and deprived of her husband's happiness. (32)
If Rāhu is situated in the eighth house, the woman will be ugly, deprived of a husband, hard-hearted, afflicted by diseases, and unchaste.
When the Moon and Venus are in the ascendant conjoined with Mars and Saturn, that woman becomes barren, provided the fifth house is aspected by or joined with malefic planets.
If Saturn, aspected by [another] Saturn, occupies the portion of Mars in the seventh house, the woman will have diseased genitals;
however, if it occupies a benefic portion in the seventh house, she should be known as fortunate and beloved by her husband. (35)
O twice-born one, if at birth Mercury is in the ascendant and conjoined with the Moon and Venus, that woman should be known to reside in her father's house and to be endowed with all happiness. (36)
If the Moon, Mercury, and Venus are in the ascendant, she will be endowed with much happiness and virtues;
if Jupiter is there, she will be highly prosperous and possessed of sons, wealth, and happiness. (37)
If the Moon and the Sun are situated in the eighth house from the ascendant and are each in their own signs, then [the woman] will be barren;
likewise, if the Moon and Mercury are so situated, she will be a "crow-barren" (kākabandhyā) woman.
If the ascendant is a sign of Saturn or Mars, and is conjoined with the Moon and Venus, yet aspected by malefic planets, that woman will certainly be barren. (39)
If Rāhu is in the seventh house and the fifth house is conjoined with malefic planets,
and Venus, Jupiter, and Rāhu are in the eighth house, she will be one whose children have died.
If Venus and Jupiter are in the eighth house, or Mars is in the seventh house conjoined with or aspected by Saturn, the woman is said to be one whose fetus miscarries. (41)
If a girl is born when the Moon is in the ascendant of Pāpakartarī, she destroys her entire paternal lineage as well as her husband's lineage. (42)
A girl whose birth occurs under the asterisms of Sarpa, Agni, Jala, or Ṛkṣa, on Sunday or Saturday, or on the Bhadra lunar day, is known as a Viṣa-kumārī.
She whose birth chart has two auspicious planets with malefic aspects on the ascendant and two malefic planets situated in the sixth house is proclaimed as the girl named Viṣā. (44)
Born under the conjunction of Viṣa, she was one whose children died at birth and who was unfortunate;
deprived of clothing and ornaments, her mind was tormented by grief. (45)
If the lord of the seventh house, or even a benefic planet, is situated in the seventh house from the ascendant or from the Moon, it undoubtedly destroys the poison-like affliction of this yoga. (46)
If Mars is in the second, fourth, seventh, or eighth house from the ascendant, and is devoid of auspicious aspects or yogas, it kills the husband; of this there is no doubt. (47)
In whichever yoga a maiden is born who slays her husband, in that same yoga a man who is born likewise slays his wife. 48.
If a maiden who was married by a woman-killer becomes the killer of her husband, then the conjunction leading to widowhood is certainly broken. 49.
If Venus and Saturn are situated in each other's signs and aspect each other,
or if they are in the sign of Venus (Virgo) with the Ascendant in the ninth part (navāṃśa) of Aquarius, the woman experiences an intensely blazing fire of passion.
O best of the twice-born, she brings peace through women who are happy yet afflicted by passion, and through others who exist in the form of men.
If Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are strong in an even sign in the ascendant,
that woman is skilled in many scriptures and is a speaker of Brahman.
If a malefic planet is in the seventh house and some planet is in the ninth,
then one attains that state of renunciation (pravrajyā) which arises from sinful planets.

If a benefic planet is situated in the eighth house from the ascendant, free from the aspect or conjunction of malefics, his death should be known to have occurred previously; of this there is no doubt. (54)
If, in the eighth house, both a benefic and a malefic are of equal strength,
then having met death along with her husband, she will certainly go to heaven.
The End of India
